name: Teylers Museum
overview: Museum of art and science at Spaarne 16 in Haarlem, with fossils, scientific instruments, books, coins, prints and drawings.

Named for Pieter Teyler (1702 to 1778), a Haarlem silk merchant and banker, out of whose will it grew and whose foundation was run by five of his friends. The Oval Room opened in 1784, which makes it the oldest museum in the Netherlands (stated by the space).
Teylers Stichting, the foundation set up by his will, owns the buildings and the collections.
funding_verdict: Teylers Museum: mixed: a state subsidy for about a third, the rest from tickets, friends, funds and a lottery
wider_context: The museum's own annual report says Pieter Teyler's surviving accounts show that part of his investments was related to slavery.
His fortune founded Teylers Stichting, which still owns the museum's buildings and collections.

name: TENT Rotterdam
overview: Contemporary art space and production house for Rotterdam artists at Coolhaven 32, in Delfshaven, with a fixed venue and nomadic projects around the city; it is a programme of CBK Rotterdam (stated by the space).
CBK Rotterdam's exhibition platform, first on the Nieuwe Binnenweg and later at Villa Alckmaer, became TENT in 1999 at Witte de Withstraat 50; TENT moved to the Coolhaven in 2024 (CBK Rotterdam).

Building: Dr. Aart Verwey founded a laboratory for testing ores, food and farm produce in 1901, and it moved into a purpose-built building at Coolhaven 32 in 1953, where it grew to about 110 staff under three generations of the Boddaert family; a fire broke out in the fume-cupboard area in 2012 (stated by the space, from research by historian Ferrie Weeda).
funding_verdict: TENT Rotterdam: mainly public: City of Rotterdam subsidy through CBK Rotterdam

name: Kunstfort bij Vijfhuizen
overview: Art centre in the Fort bij Vijfhuizen, at Fortwachter 1 on the edge of Haarlemmermeer, close to Schiphol airport (stated by the Kunstfort).

The fort was built in 1889 to 1890 as one of the forts of the Stelling van Amsterdam, a defence line laid out between 1880 and 1914 (Wikipedia; Kunstfort). The line has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1996.
The fort lost its military function in 1963 and has had an artistic one since 2005 (stated by the Kunstfort).
funding_verdict: Kunstfort bij Vijfhuizen: public grants: Mondriaan Fund and, as stated by the Kunstfort, the municipality of Haarlemmermeer

name: Museum Voorlinden
overview: A privately run museum for modern and contemporary art at Buurtweg 90 in Wassenaar, on the Voorlinden estate of woods, dunes and gardens, which visitors can walk (museum website).

Joop van Caldenborgh, born in The Hague in 1940 and founder of the chemical company Caldic, opened it in 2016; he gave the collection, the museum and the estate to the Voorlinden Foundation, and what he buys since is added to the gift (Ara, 11 September 2026).

What is there: thousands of works gathered by Van Caldenborgh, with pieces by Damien Hirst, Richard Serra, Louise Bourgeois, Anish Kapoor, James Turrell, Maurizio Cattelan, Pipilotti Rist, Anselm Kiefer and Yayoi Kusama; the director Suzanne Swarts says 'We collect 21st-century art and we want to make it dialogue with that of the 20th century'. The tenth-anniversary exhibition of 2026 shows about 100 works with loans from the Centre Pompidou, the Stedelijk, the Beyeler Foundation and others (Ara, 11 September 2026).
funding_verdict: Museum Voorlinden: private, the founder's gift and yearly donations plus tickets, shop and restaurant; no subsidy

name: World Heritage Rock Art Centre – Alta Museum (Verdensarvsenter for bergkunst – Alta Museum)
overview: Museum and world heritage centre at Hjemmeluft, about 5 km west of central Alta in Finnmark, beside one of the five rock art areas inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 (Alta Museum).

Founded in 1978 as a municipal museum, it moved into a new building at Hjemmeluft in 1991 and became an intermunicipal company in 1997 (Store norske leksikon); the first rock carvings at Hjemmeluft were found in 1973 (Store norske leksikon).
The museum building went up in two stages, finished in 1991 and 2013; most of the buildings the museum uses belong to Alta Municipality (economic plan 2026 to 2029).
funding_verdict: Alta Museum: mainly public: Alta Municipality, Finnmark County and the Norwegian state, plus ticket, shop and café sales

name: Festspillene i Nord-Norge (Arctic Arts Festival)
overview: An eight-day international festival of music, theatre, dance and visual art held in Harstad each June around the summer solstice (festival). The 2026 edition ran from 20 to 27 June; the next runs from 19 to 26 June 2027 (festival).

The journalist Jan Kr. Nilssen called a meeting at the Grand Hotel in Harstad on 8 April 1964, which chose an interim board; the first official meeting followed on 22 June 1964, and the first festival opened on 5 June 1965 (festival history page).
It is organised by the foundation Festspillene i Nord-Norge, which has eight employees (Brønnøysund Register).
funding_verdict: Festspillene i Nord-Norge: mainly public: the state, the three northern counties and Harstad, with business partners
wider_context: The festival reported a financial fraud linked to the 2017 festival to the police; its loss came to 82,400 euros, about NOK 770,000 (Fagforbundet, 29 September 2017).

name: Kunstnernes Hus
overview: Artist-run exhibition house at Wergelandsveien 17 in Oslo. Its own site calls it Norway's oldest artist-run institution, non-commercial and independent since 1930.

Norwegian artists founded and built it. It is owned by Norway's artists, organised in the professional artists' organisations (Kunstnernes Hus). A council of members from eight artists' organisations appoints the board of the foundation Stiftelsen Kunstnernes Hus (annual report 2024).
It opened on 1 October 1930 with the Autumn Exhibition (Høstutstillingen), attended by King Haakon. It had cost 650,000 kroner (museum history page).
funding_verdict: Kunstnernes Hus: operating grants from the Ministry of Culture and the City of Oslo, with foundation support; Sparebankstiftelsen DNB gave the start of the rehabilitation funding

name: Stavanger kunstmuseum
overview: An art museum at Henrik Ibsens gate 55 by Mosvannet in Stavanger, in a building by the architect Per Faltinsen, run as the art department of Museum Stavanger AS (MUST), which provides shared finance, staff, marketing and collection services (museum website; MUST annual report 2025).

Its roots are in Stavanger kunstforening's permanent gallery, begun on 11 February 1865 when consul Jens Z. Kielland became chairman; in 1966 local government took over and the collection became the foundation Stavanger Faste Galleri, renamed Rogaland kunstmuseum in 1990 and Stavanger kunstmuseum in 2010 (museum website).

What is there: the museum's page gives the collection as 3,500 artworks in its introduction and 'over 2,600 works' in its history section; it holds Norway's largest collection of Lars Hertervig, a growing group of paintings by Kitty Kielland, works by Frida Hansen, the Jan Groth collection begun in 1998 with gifts from the artist and added to by Steingrim Laursen's bequest in 2007, and 67 contemporary works given by Trond Mohn in autumn 2012 (museum website).
funding_verdict: Stavanger kunstmuseum: mainly public, through the municipally and county owned Museum Stavanger AS, plus foundations and local donors

name: Lofoten International Art Festival (LIAF)
overview: A contemporary art biennial for Northern Norway with a history going back to 1991; it began with a regional and national focus and has no fixed venue, having shown art in a park, a garage, a library, a bunker, a fishing hut and a private house (North Norwegian Art Centre).
Since 2009 it has been organised by the North Norwegian Art Centre (NNKS) in Svolvær with a LIAF Steering Committee chaired by Karolin Tampere; the centre's director is Luba Kuzovnikova (NNKS).

NNKS was founded in 1979 by the artists' associations Nord-Norske Bildende Kunstnere and Norske Kunsthåndverkere Nord-Norge; it runs a gallery and sales of art and crafts in Svolvær and the residency house Kunstnerhuset Svolvær on Svinøya (NNKS).
funding_verdict: LIAF: mainly public: Arts Council Norway, the northern counties and Vågan Municipality, with foundation, embassy and bank grants for each edition

name: Khalil Sakakini Cultural Center
overview: Palestinian arts and culture centre in Ramallah, housed in a renovated early-20th-century building in traditional Palestinian style (stated by the centre).
Established in May 1996 as a branch of the Palestinian Ministry of Culture and registered as a non-profit NGO in 1998 (stated by the centre).
Named for Khalil Sakakini, described by Wikipedia as a Jerusalemite scholar, poet and nationalist.
funding_verdict: Khalil Sakakini Cultural Center: donor-funded: international grants and foundation support
wider_context: Jadaliyya (13 April 2022, a partisan pro-Palestinian outlet) reports that on 12 January 2022 a DIE ZEIT editor asked "Does the Documenta have an anti-Semitism problem?" and made allegations against Yazan Khalili, spokesman of The Question of Funding, tying the group in part to the Khalil Sakakini Cultural Center and calling Sakakini a "radical nationalist and Nazi supporter". Jadaliyya also reports that the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung published an article on 14 January 2022 about "Hetzkunst" (translation: incitement art) to be shown at documenta fifteen.

Unverified: Ruhrbarone and a Dortmund website claimed that Sakakini supported National Socialism, from Jadaliyya, which says the claim feeds the newspaper columns and argues that his diaries do not support it.
The ZEIT editor tied his group to the centre and to its namesake.

name: Cricoteka (Centre for the Documentation of the Art of Tadeusz Kantor)
overview: Museum, archive, gallery and research centre devoted to the director and painter Tadeusz Kantor (1915 to 1990), in the Podgórze district of Kraków at ul. Nadwiślańska 2-4. It also runs the Galeria-Pracownia Tadeusza Kantora at ul. Sienna 7/5.
Founded in Kraków in 1980 on Kantor's initiative as a "living archive" of his Cricot 2 theatre, which Kantor co-founded in 1955 with Maria Jarema and Kazimierz Mikulski (stated by the space).
Polish Wikipedia says Cricot 2 rehearsed in the basement of a chapter house and that Cricoteka was at ul. Szczepańska 2 until 2014. Natalia Zarzecka has directed it since 2004 (Polish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Cricoteka: mainly public: Małopolska Voivodeship, with the building co-financed by the European Union

name: Wrocław Contemporary Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum at pl. Strzegomski 2 in Wrocław, in a cylindrical six-storey air-raid shelter about 25 metres high and 31 metres across, built in 1942 to designs by the Wrocław architect Richard Konwiarz (stated by the museum).
The shelter served as a field hospital during the 1945 siege of Festung Breslau and after 1989 housed wholesalers, supermarkets, a pub and a second-hand clothes shop (stated by the museum).

Wrocław City Council created the museum by resolution VI/66/11 of 10 February 2011 as a municipal cultural institution; its aim is to build and show an international collection of contemporary art (notes to the 2024 accounts). It has been in the shelter since 2011 (stated by the museum).
funding_verdict: Wrocław Contemporary Museum: public: the City of Wrocław, with Culture Ministry grants for acquisitions

name: Culturgest
overview: Arts centre and foundation (Culturgest, Fundação Caixa Geral de Depósitos) at Rua Arco do Cego 50, Lisbon, in the head-office building of Caixa Geral de Depósitos (CGD). Campo Pequeno metro station is about 450 m away. A second venue operates in Porto.
Set up by Caixa Geral de Depósitos, a state-owned financial group, as a private foundation. It opened to the public in October 1993 (stated by the foundation).

Programme: performing arts, music, visual arts, cinema and contemporary thought, plus lectures, debates, workshops, guided tours and programmes for schools and families. It also holds and catalogues the CGD art collection online.
funding_verdict: Culturgest: corporate-foundation funded: Caixa Geral de Depósitos, a state-owned bank

name: Galeria Zé dos Bois (ZDB)
overview: Non-profit cultural association and art centre in a 2,500 m2 palace at Rua da Barroca 59 in the Bairro Alto, Lisbon, with a second venue, ZDB 8 Marvila (stated by ZDB).

Created in 1994 as a non-profit by a civic initiative of fifteen founders, who wanted an alternative structure to the institutional and commercial panorama (stated by ZDB). Natxo Checa is one of the founders and the current director (Observador, Agência Lusa, 29 November 2024).

Programmes: visual arts exhibitions. NEGÓCIO, for performing arts, with about 12 premieres a year. ZDBmüzique, for experimental, improvised and electroacoustic music. An education service founded in 2005. A bookshop and a rooftop terrace (stated by ZDB). ZDB says it hosts more than 150 events a year.
funding_verdict: Galeria Zé dos Bois (ZDB): public and earned income: Direção-Geral das Artes, Lisbon City Council and paid attendance at shows and exhibitions

name: Museu Nacional Soares dos Reis
aliases: Museu Nacional de Soares dos Reis
overview: A national museum of art in the Palácio dos Carrancas on Rua de D. Manuel II in Porto, with a second site, the Casa-Museu Fernando de Castro, at Rua Costa Cabral 716 (museum website; Renascença, 6 October 2025).

It was inaugurated in 1833 as the Museu Portuense, in the Convento de Santo António da Cidade, when King Pedro IV decided to set up a museum of paintings and prints in the city (Renascença, 6 October 2025; museum collections page).

What is there: more than 18,000 pieces, including about 2,500 paintings from the 16th to the 20th century (Silva Porto, Marques de Oliveira, Henrique Pousão, Aurélia de Souza, António Carneiro), sculpture centred on Soares dos Reis and his 'O Desterrado' (Rome, 1872), northern Portuguese faience, glass, jewellery, textiles and furniture; ten pieces are classed as National Treasures. The first holdings came from church and convent property confiscated during the Liberal Wars and the Siege of Porto (1832 to 1833), later joined by the Museu Municipal do Porto's collection, deposited in 1937 (museum collections page).
funding_verdict: Museu Nacional Soares dos Reis: public, a state museum under Museus e Monumentos de Portugal, with EU recovery money for the building and patrons for the programme

name: DK Rozy (Rosa's House of Culture)
overview: Social centre and School of Engaged Art run by the artist collective Chto Delat in Saint Petersburg. The house has not operated since 2022 (Chto Delat, June 2023).

Chto Delat was founded in early 2003 in Saint Petersburg. The collective's main page dates Rosa's House of Culture to 2013, alongside the School of Engaged Art. Its project page says the House "opens its door on 1st of May in 2015" (Chto Delat website).

The name follows the Soviet House of Culture model. The pages opened do not say whom "Rosa" honours. Chto Delat researched the history of Soviet Houses of Culture from 2016 (Garage Museum project page).
funding_verdict: DK Rozy: mainly self-funded by the collective: Mutual Aid Fund, participant donations and grants

press_items.title: A Journal of Socially-Engaged Art Criticism: Anastasia Vepreva, Dmitry Vilensky, Roman Osminkin and Jozhi Stolet, "A Discussion with Residents of Rosa House of Culture" (2019)

name: Kigali Genocide Memorial
overview: A memorial and documentation centre on a hillside in Gisozi, Kigali, with mass graves beside the memorial buildings (memorial website).
It opened in 2004. The Kigali City Council owns the land and invited the Aegis Trust in 2003 to establish it (memorial website).

What is there: the final resting place for 250,000 victims of the genocide against the Tutsi, exhibitions and survivors' testimony, and virtual 360 degree tours. The pages read do not give an object count.
funding_verdict: Kigali Genocide Memorial: donor funded through the Aegis Trust, with foreign governments, foundations and Rwandan companies
wider_context: The memorial is managed by a foreign charity for a government ministry on land owned by the city council (memorial website, partnerships page).

name: Constitution Hill
overview: An urban regeneration project in Johannesburg that hosts the Constitutional Court and the Old Fort Prison Complex (Johannesburg Development Agency).
The Johannesburg Development Agency delivered it; the pages read do not state the opening dates.

What is there: Number Four held many political detainees before 1994, including Mahatma Gandhi and Nelson Mandela, and the site offers education on constitutionalism, human rights and democracy, with office space for NGOs and Chapter Nine bodies (Johannesburg Development Agency; Constitution Hill website).
funding_verdict: Constitution Hill: public capital from province and city, with foundation grants for the Trust's programmes

name: Sun Mu Studio & North Korean Dissident Art Archive
overview: The working base and website of the pseudonymous North Korean defector artist Sun Mu, who lives in South Korea. A Korean article reproduced on his site places his studio near Haengju Fortress by the Han River in Goyang, in an area bordered by a military fence.

Sun Mu is a pseudonym meaning "no borders" (Wende Museum). He was trained as a propaganda-poster artist, left North Korea in 1998 according to the Wende Museum, and still works in that style, turning its messages upside down. A 2008 Weekly Kyunghyang profile says he left in 2002 and entered Hongik University in 2003. The sources disagree on the year.
His site names his work as portraits of life in North Korea and "images of hope" (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: Sun Mu Studio: self-funded as an individual artist's practice, with project support from outside groups
wider_context: Beijing, 2014: Chinese police blocked entry to Sun Mu's show "Red White Blue" at Yuan Dian gallery and removed the paintings shortly before its 27 July opening, and officials gave no reason (The Verge, 30 July 2014, citing Yonhap, as reproduced on sunmuart.com). A Korean article reproduced on the same page (JoongAng Ilbo) says Chinese security officers raided the gallery after a North Korean embassy report and seized about 80 works and 1,000 catalogues.
China neither funds nor controls the studio; the action fell on an exhibition in China.

press_items.title: "North Korean Defector Artist Sun Mu's Lost Utopias" (undated, author not named; image file names point to February 2019)
event recap, "Sun Mu: From North Korean Propagandist to Pop Art Defector" (undated)

name: Espacio Fundación Telefónica
overview: A free exhibition and events space of 6,000 square metres on four floors of the Telefónica building on Gran Vía in Madrid, with its entrance at Calle Fuencarral 3 (Espacio website).

Fundación Telefónica opened it in 2012; the building, by the company's architect Ignacio de Cárdenas, was finished on 1 January 1930, and the foundation and the studio Quanto Arquitectura coordinated its restoration (Espacio website). The foundation itself was constituted by Telefónica, S.A. on 25 June 1998, with its seat at Gran Vía 28 (annual accounts 2024).

What is there: temporary exhibitions on floors 3 and 4, a permanent exhibition on the history of telecommunications and an auditorium on floor 2 (Espacio website). The Colección Telefónica brings together works of art, technological objects, photographs, documents and audiovisual archives; its art collection, begun in the 1980s with works by Picasso, Juan Gris, Tàpies and Chillida, holds more than 1,100 pieces, with Cubism as its core (María Blanchard, Jean Metzinger), Surrealist holdings (Magritte, Matta) and contemporary photography (foundation collections page). Telefónica, S.A. gave the foundation a capital donation of 15 million dollars (15,550,487 euros) in 1999 to buy modern and contemporary painting and photography (annual accounts 2024).
funding_verdict: Espacio Fundación Telefónica: corporate, paid by Telefónica, S.A. through its foundation
